decks.title: A quarter of your needs every other day: 12 weeks in adults without obesity

slides.heading: Does fasting every other day work if you're not obese?
slides.body: Adults ate one meal of 400 to 600 kcal every other day, for 12 weeks.

slides.heading: After 12 weeks, the fasting group weighed 5.2 kg less.
slides.body: Most of it was fat: 3.6 kg.

slides.heading: Free days did not refill the gap.
slides.body: On free days they ate about what the control group ate, with little catch-up eating (hyperphagia).

slides.heading: Tested in 30 adults without obesity.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Groups set by a random draw; body fat scanned.
art.weak: Small, and groups merged after the fact.

slides.heading: Could you eat one small meal every other day?
slides.body: Compare weight and fat lost against the control group.

slide.heading: What do 12 weeks of every-other-day fasting do?
slide.body: Adults without obesity ate one small meal on alternate days.

decks.caption: A randomized trial in 30 adults without obesity. Every other day, the fasting group ate one meal of 400 to 600 kcal. After 12 weeks, they weighed 5.2 kg less than the control group. Small, 12 weeks, and the authors merged the groups after the fact. Full read and the weight explorer: link in bio.
decks.credit: Varady KA, Bhutani S, Klempel MC, Kroeger CM, Trepanowski JF, Haus JM, Hoddy KK, Calvo Y. Alternate day fasting for weight loss in normal weight and overweight subjects: a randomized controlled trial. Nutr J. 2013;12:146. doi:10.1186/1475-2891-12-146 doi:10.1186/1475-2891-12-146. Licence: CC-BY.

decks.title: Brushing as well as you can, once: what a dentist found on 91 students

slides.heading: Does trying your best at the sink get teeth cleaner?
slides.body: Students brushed as thoroughly as they could, or as usual, then dentists checked.

slides.heading: Gumline plaque: no clear difference from brushing as usual.
slides.body: Trying hard added nearly a minute, mostly on the outer surfaces.

slides.heading: More time, same blind spots.
slides.body: Two-thirds skipped a section of the mouth (sextant). One in ten never brushed the tongue side.

slides.heading: Tested on students, after one brushing.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Instruction set by lot; dentists did not know which.
art.missing: Weeks of trying harder: not studied.

slides.heading: Where does your brushing time go?
slides.body: Compare how each group split its time between surfaces.

slide.heading: How many people floss the way dentists mean?
slide.body: In a filmed trial, this many in each group got it right.

slide.heading: Does brushing your best clean between your teeth?
slide.body: After students brushed their best, plaque stayed on this share of the gumline between teeth.

figure.label: of between-teeth gumline sections kept plaque

decks.caption: A randomized trial of 111 university students told to brush as well as they could, or as usual. The best-effort group brushed nearly a minute longer. Plaque along the gumline afterwards showed no clear difference. Both groups thought their teeth were about twice as clean as the dentists found. One brushing session, students only. Full read and the brushing-time explorer: link in bio.
decks.credit: Weik U, Shankar-Subramanian S, Sämann T, Wöstmann B, Margraf-Stiksrud J, Deinzer R. “You should brush your teeth better”: a randomized controlled trial comparing best-possible versus as-usual toothbrushing. BMC Oral Health. 2023;23. doi:10.1186/s12903-023-03127-3 doi:10.1186/s12903-023-03127-3. Licence: CC-BY.

study.cite: Weik et al., BMC Oral Health

decks.title: A ceramide cream and cleanser for eczema, against a placebo set for 28 days

slides.heading: Does a ceramide cream beat a plain cream for eczema?
slides.body: Adults with moderate eczema used one or the other twice a day, for 28 days.

slides.heading: On the eczema score, no clear difference after 28 days.
slides.body: But the ceramide set kept more water in the skin.

slides.heading: Ceramides are part of the mortar between skin cells.
slides.body: Eczema skin holds less, so water escapes (transepidermal water loss).

slides.heading: Tested in 100 adults with moderate eczema.
How sure can we be?

art.weak: Run by the cream's maker; 28 days only.

slides.heading: Is your moisturizer doing the mortar's job?
slides.body: Compare the eczema scores for both sets, start to finish.

slide.heading: Can a cream patch the mortar between skin cells?
slide.body: Adults with eczema tried a ceramide cream and cleanser.

decks.caption: A randomized, double-blind trial in 100 adults with moderate eczema. After 28 days, the eczema score showed no clear difference between a ceramide cream and cleanser and a placebo set. Water loss through the skin fell more with the ceramide set. Run by the cream's maker. Full read: link in bio.
decks.credit: Spada F, Harrison IP, Barnes TM, Greive KA, Daniels D, Townley JP, Mostafa N, Fong AT, Tong PL, Shumack S. A daily regimen of a ceramide-dominant moisturizing cream and cleanser restores the skin permeability barrier in adults with moderate eczema: A randomized trial. Dermatol Ther. 2021;34(4):e14970. doi:10.1111/dth.14970 doi:10.1111/dth.14970. Licence: CC-BY.

decks.title: Caffeine three times a day, the last dose 8 hours before bed: what the sleep lab recorded

slides.heading: Is coffee after noon bad for your sleep?
slides.body: The usual advice: stop by noon. A sleep lab gave caffeine until mid-afternoon, daily for 10 days.

slides.heading: Their sleep showed no clear difference from placebo nights.
slides.body: Each dose was 150 mg, about a cup and a half of coffee.

slides.heading: They were already heavy caffeine users.
slides.body: Each had 300 to 600 mg a day. Daily use blunts its effect on sleep.

slides.heading: Only if you look like the people tested.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Double-blind, and each man had every condition.
art.weak: Only twenty people, all young men.
art.missing: No sizes given for the differences.

slides.heading: When is your last coffee?
slides.body: Put in your wake time and coffee times. See how your day compares with the one this lab tested.

slide.heading: How much coffee did the sleep lab give?
slide.body: Three doses a day, each about a cup and a half, for 10 days.

decks.caption: A double-blind crossover trial in twenty young men: caffeine three times a day, ending 8 hours before bed. Their measured sleep showed no clear difference from placebo. A small trial in men aged 18 to 35, and the text gives no sizes for the differences. Simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Weibel J, Lin YS, Landolt HP, et al. The impact of daily caffeine intake on nighttime sleep in young adult men. Sci Rep. 2021;11(1):4668. doi:10.1038/s41598-021-84088-x. Licence: CC-BY.

decks.title: Interval training's best-supported effect is on lean mass, not fat: thirty-six trials, graded

slides.heading: Is interval training mostly about fat loss?
slides.body: Ads say so. Thirty-six trials, pooled and graded for how far each result can be trusted.

slides.heading: Less fat mass. A little more lean mass.
slides.body: Against no exercise, after 3 to 15 weeks.

slides.heading: Your weight is two piles on one scale.
slides.body: One is fat. The other, lean mass, is muscle, bone, organs and water.

slides.heading: It describes inactive adults with extra weight best.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Thirty-six chance-assigned trials; lean mass graded high.
art.weak: Without one trial, the lean-mass gain is unclear.

slides.heading: Build your own interval plan
slides.body: Pick an interval type and rest. See the estimate for each choice.

slide.heading: What did interval training do to fat and lean mass?
slide.body: Thirty-six trials against no exercise, 3 to 15 weeks each.

decks.caption: Thirty-six randomized trials of interval training in adults, pooled and graded. Body fat percentage fell by 1.53 points, at low certainty. Fat-free mass rose by 0.51 kg, at high certainty, though the result depends on one trial. Full read and simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Khodadadi F, Bagheri R, Negaresh R, et al. The Effect of High-Intensity Interval Training Type on Body Fat Percentage, Fat and Fat-Free Mass: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. J Clin Med. 2023;12(6):2291. doi:10.3390/jcm12062291. Licence: CC-BY.

study.cite: Khodadadi et al., Journal of Clinical Medicine

decks.title: Two weeks of longer sleep at home: what 80 adults then ate

slides.heading: Can more sleep mean eating less?
slides.body: No diet, no exercise plan: 80 short sleepers aimed for 8.5 hours in bed.

a.label: their usual sleep was under this

slides.heading: The longer sleepers ate 270.4 kcal a day less.
slides.body: Compared with the control group, over 2 weeks.

slides.heading: Weight is a ledger: food in, energy out.
slides.body: Food in fell. Energy out showed no clear change. So the balance tipped.

slides.heading: Only if you look like the people tested.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Groups set by chance; energy measured, not self-reported.
art.missing: Why they ate less: not studied.

slides.heading: When do you go to bed?
slides.body: See your own bedtime against the 8.5 hours they aimed for.

slide.heading: What happened when short sleepers slept longer?
slide.body: Against the control group, they ate this much less a day.

decks.caption: A randomized trial of 80 adults with overweight who slept under 6.5 hours a night. Sleep advice gave the sleep group 1.2 hours more sleep a night than the control group. Those adults ate 270.4 kcal a day less than the control group, with no diet. The control group also ate 114.9 kcal a day more than before, and the change lasted 2 weeks. Full read and the estimate explorer: link in bio.

Effect of Sleep Extension on Objectively Assessed Energy Intake Among Adults With Overweight in Real-life Settings: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2022;182(4):365-374. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.8098. Licence: CC-BY.

decks.title: Five short nights: how appealing sweets looked to 31 teens

slides.heading: Do short nights give teens a sweet tooth?
slides.body: Teens spent five nights with 6.5 hours in bed and five with 10, then rated food photos.

slides.heading: After short nights, teens rated sweets as more appealing.
slides.body: Hunger showed no clear difference.

slides.heading: Short sleep may turn up how good sweets look.
slides.body: The authors' idea: sweets promise more pleasure (hedonic value) after short nights.

slides.heading: Tested in 31 teens, over five short nights.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Each teen did both schedules, in random order.
art.weak: Small, and only five short nights.

slides.heading: What time do you go to bed?
slides.body: Compare calories and sweets after each kind of night.

slide.heading: What do five short nights do to a sweet tooth?
slide.body: 31 teens rated food photos after short and long nights.

decks.caption: A randomized crossover trial in 31 teens aged 14 to 17. Each spent five nights with 6.5 hours in bed and five with 10. After the short nights, they rated sweets and desserts as more appealing. Hunger showed no clear difference. Small, and measured only after five short nights. Full read and the calorie explorer: link in bio.
decks.credit: Simon SL, Field J, Miller LE, DiFrancesco M, Beebe DW. Sweet/dessert foods are more appealing to adolescents after sleep restriction. PLoS One. 2015;10(2):e0115434. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0115434 doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0115434. Licence: CC-BY.

study.span: five short and five long nights each

decks.title: 8,000 steps on one or two days a week: what ten years of death records show

slides.heading: Do you need 8,000 steps every day?
slides.body: Most step goals are daily. This study counted how many days a week 3,101 adults reached 8,000.

figure.label: on how many days a week?

slides.heading: One or two such days a week went with a lower risk of death.
slides.body: Over 10 years, against people with none.

slides.heading: The risk gap opens fast, then levels off.
slides.body: It levelled off at 3 to 4 days a week.

slides.heading: Only if you look like the people tested.
How sure can we be?

art.weak: Poor health can mean fewer steps and earlier death.

slides.heading: How many 8,000-step days do you get?
slides.body: Count your step days last week. Find your group in the simulator.

slide.heading: What went with one or two 8,000-step days a week?
slide.body: A risk of death this much lower over 10 years than having none.

slide.heading: Is more always better for step days?
slide.body: Among 3,101 adults, the risk gap levelled off at 3 to 4 days a week.

slide.heading: Does your daily step goal matter much?
slide.body: This study also tried goals from 6000 to 10 000 steps a day. They gave similar results.

decks.caption: A 10-year follow-up of 3,101 US adults. Reaching 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week was associated with a risk of death 14.9 points lower than never reaching it. An observational study, and the groups differed in age and health. Source and simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Inoue K, Tsugawa Y, Mayeda ER, Ritz B. Association of Daily Step Patterns With Mortality in US Adults. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(3):e235174. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.5174. Licence: CC-BY.

study.cite: Inoue et al., JAMA Network Open

decks.title: Fructose or glucose: what pooled trials found for an inflammation marker

slides.heading: Does fructose fan inflammation more than other sugars?
slides.body: A review pooled trials that gave people fructose or the same calories of glucose.

slides.heading: Fructose and glucose: no clear difference in CRP.
slides.body: CRP is a blood protein used as a marker of inflammation.

slides.heading: Fructose goes to the liver, where some can become fat.
slides.body: The theory: by-products of that fat may set off inflammation (lipotoxicity).

slides.heading: Tested in 13 controlled trials.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Every trial had a control group; review registered first.
art.weak: Low certainty: few trials, wide ranges.

slides.heading: Where does your sugar come from?
slides.body: See how wide each pooled range is.

slide.heading: Does fructose inflame more than glucose?
slide.body: Any cell can burn glucose; fructose has to go to the liver.

decks.caption: A review pooled 13 controlled trials with 1141 people. CRP, a blood marker of inflammation, showed no clear difference between fructose and glucose. Corn syrup against table sugar: no clear difference either. Certainty is low: few trials, short ones, often at very large doses. Full read and the range explorer: link in bio.
decks.credit: Della Corte KW, Perrar I, Penczynski KJ, Schwingshackl L, Herder C, Buyken AE. Effect of Dietary Sugar Intake on Biomarkers of Subclinical Inflammation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Intervention Studies. Nutrients. 2018;10(5):606. doi:10.3390/nu10050606 doi:10.3390/nu10050606. Licence: CC-BY.

study.span: 2 weeks to 3 months of sugar each

decks.title: Same 8 hours, different clock: what changed in 82 adults over five weeks

slides.heading: Does it matter when you eat, within the same 8 hours?
slides.body: Adults ate early, at mid-day, or as usual, for five weeks.

slides.heading: In these adults, only the early window clearly lowered insulin resistance.
slides.body: Both window groups ate less, by amounts with no clear difference.

slides.heading: Same hours of eating, a different time of day.
slides.body: The authors suggest the body's daily rhythms (circadian clock) may play a part.

slides.heading: Tested in healthy adults, for five weeks.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Groups set by chance; outcome measurers blinded.
art.weak: Small, short, and participants knew their group.

slides.heading: When is your last bite of the day?
slides.body: Compare each group's weight change after five weeks.

slide.heading: Can eating earlier in the day change your weight?
slide.body: Healthy adults ate between 6:00 and 15:00 for five weeks.

decks.caption: A randomized trial of 82 healthy adults over five weeks. One group ate within 8 hours between 6:00 and 15:00, another between 11:00 and 20:00, a third as usual. Only the early group's insulin resistance fell more than the other groups'. Both window groups ate less, with no clear difference between them. Small, short, and participants knew their group. Full read and the weight explorer: link in bio.
decks.credit: Xie Z, Sun Y, Ye Y, Hu D, Zhang H, He Z, Zhao H, Yang H, Mao Y. Randomized controlled trial for time-restricted eating in healthy volunteers without obesity. Nat Commun. 2022;13. doi:10.1038/s41467-022-28662-5 doi:10.1038/s41467-022-28662-5. Licence: CC-BY.

decks.title: 1 g of black pepper in breakfast: what blood glucose did over the next 3 hours

slides.heading: Can black pepper change your breakfast blood sugar?
slides.body: 20 healthy adults ate the same egg breakfast, with and without black pepper.

figure.label: of black pepper, in the egg

slides.heading: Blood sugar ran lower after the pepper meals.
slides.body: The clear gap was at the 30-minute reading.

slides.heading: A doorbell in your mouth
slides.body: Food presses it, and the body hears a meal is coming. The authors say pepper might press it.

slides.heading: Only if you look like the people tested.
How sure can we be?

art.strong: Each person ate all four breakfasts, in random order.
art.weak: Single meals; lower hunger may reflect taste.
art.missing: No sizes given for the differences.

slides.heading: Which breakfast would you pick?
slides.body: Pick a meal in the simulator to see what the trial recorded.

slide.heading: When did the pepper meals show a blood sugar gap?
slide.body: 20 healthy adults ate egg breakfasts with and without black pepper.

figure.label: after eating: the one clear gap

decks.caption: A crossover trial in 20 healthy young adults tested 1 g of black pepper in a breakfast egg. Blood glucose was lower at 30 minutes than after the plain meal. Over 3 hours the meals showed no clear difference, nor did turmeric alone. The text does not say how big any difference was. Simulator at the link in bio.
decks.credit: Khan S, Arif M, Laraib H, et al. The effect of turmeric and black pepper powder incorporated in breakfast on postprandial glycemia, appetite, palatability, and gastrointestinal well-being in normal-weight adults. Food Sci Nutr. 2024;12(4):2846-2854. doi:10.1002/fsn3.3965. Licence: CC-BY.
